title: Rich Tasks / Three-Act Math
subtitle: A compelling problem students reason their way through, then consolidate into formal mathematics. The centerpiece of Core Instruction — and the destination the opener routines rehearse for.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Dan Meyer, Three-Act Math · Make Math Moments 3-Part Framework · Smith & Stein, 5 Practices (2011) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Liljedahl, Building Thinking Classrooms (2020).

blocks.text: A **rich task** is a problem with a **low floor and a high ceiling** — every student can start it, and it can be taken surprisingly far. Students do the reasoning *before* the teacher formalizes the math.

**Three-Act Math** (Dan Meyer; mirrored in Make Math Moments’ 3-part framework) is the most powerful structure for delivering one. It withholds information and the question at first, sparks a real need to know, lets students struggle productively, and then pays the curiosity off with a reveal. This is the opposite of the typical word problem, where the method is shown and students mimic it.
The three acts

rows: A short visual, video, or scenario with very little information. The class notices and wonders.
Generate the question themselves, then commit to an **estimate** — a guess, plus a “too low” and “too high.” Everyone has a stake.
Students decide what information they need, ask for it, and work toward a solution. The teacher monitors and questions.
Reason, try strategies, struggle productively, use multiple representations. This is where the mathematics gets *made*, not received.
The answer is revealed (often a video/image), then the teacher consolidates — formalizing the math from selected student strategies. Sequel questions extend it.
Check their estimate against reality, connect strategies, name the formal mathematics, and push further with the sequel.

blocks.text: Every move teachers built in the 10-minute opener routines — eliciting strategies, revoicing, holding struggle, consolidating — now operates at full scale across a whole lesson. And rich tasks develop the one strand the openers reach least: **strategic competence** (formulating and solving genuine problems). This is where the discourse muscle pays off and where benchmark achievement realistically begins to move.
What it develops

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Strategic competence
Adaptive reasoning
Conceptual understanding
Procedural fluency
Productive disposition

blocks.text: A well-run rich task is the only routine in the toolbelt that develops all five strands at full strength in one lesson.

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Implement tasks that promote reasoning & problem solving
Support productive struggle
Establish math goals
Elicit & use evidence of thinking
Connect representations

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Students asking “what do we need to know?” — owning the question
Estimates and bounds before any computing
Multiple solution paths, not one prescribed method
Productive struggle — engaged, trying things, not rescued early
The teacher monitoring and questioning, then consolidating from student work
A genuine payoff at the reveal

no.title: We should *not* see
items: The teacher demonstrating the method, then students mimicking
One question, one path, one right approach
All the information handed over up front
A “fun activity” with no mathematics consolidated
Struggle cut short the instant a hand goes up
No formalization — the task ends without the math being named

blocks.title: The two ways rich tasks go wrong

blocks.text: **(1) No consolidation:** students explore, have fun, and never get to the formal mathematics — “activity without learning.” Act 3 (the consolidation) is non-negotiable. **(2) Fake-rich:** a normal word problem dressed up — still one path, still teacher-shown. A task is only rich if there is genuine reasoning students could not have just copied.

items: **Low floor:** the hook and the estimate let *every* student in before any formal math — a newcomer MLL can estimate and notice/wonder.
**High ceiling & multiple paths:** there are many ways to be smart, so more students get to be the one with a valued strategy.
**Curiosity is the great equalizer:** a compelling Act 1 engages students who have checked out of procedural math.

**Maintain the cognitive demand for all:** the equity risk is quietly handing struggling students a stripped-down version — instead, scaffold access (visuals, partners, stems) while keeping the task whole.

blocks.text: Don’t start here. Launch rich tasks once the opener routines are humming (see the readiness trigger in the rollout plan) — the discourse norms and the teacher’s facilitation moves built in the openers are exactly what a rich task needs. Begin with **one rich task per unit**, not daily, and grow from there.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Smith & Stein, 5 Practices for Orchestrating Productive Mathematics Discussions (2011) · Dan Meyer, Three-Act Math · Make Math Moments 3-Part Framework · Liljedahl, Building Thinking Classrooms (2020) · NCTM, Principles to Actions.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
A rich task **is** the lesson (or most of it) — the Core Instruction block, not the opener. Plan for a full period; some tasks run two days.

An opener might even prime it (a fraction Number Talk before a proportional-reasoning task), but the rich task is the main event: students reason through it, and the teacher consolidates the math from what they produce.
The engine: the 5 Practices

What separates a rich task that teaches from one that’s just fun is the teacher’s facilitation. Smith & Stein’s **5 Practices** are the planning-and-facilitation routine that makes the consolidation land. The first happens before class; the rest happen live.

items: **Anticipate (before class).** Do the math yourself. List the strategies — and misconceptions — students will likely produce. *(This is the PLC “do the math first” habit at work.)*
**Monitor (Act 2).** Circulate as students work; note who is doing what. Ask purposeful questions; resist rescuing.
**Select.** Choose specific student work to share — not volunteers, but the pieces that build the mathematical story.
**Sequence.** Order them deliberately, usually concrete/accessible → abstract, so the consolidation builds.
**Connect (Act 3).** Make the links explicit — between strategies, to the representations, and to the formal mathematics and the learning goal.

blocks.title: This is why the openers came first

blocks.text: Monitoring, selecting, sequencing, and connecting are the *same moves* a teacher rehearsed in Number Talks — just across a full task instead of a single problem. A faculty that skipped the openers will struggle here; a faculty that built the muscle will recognize the work.
A worked example: “Stacking Cups” (proportional & linear reasoning)
A classic 6–8 three-act task (ratios, rates, and `y = mx + b`; IAS 7.RP / 8.EE).

rows: Show one styrofoam cup, then stand beside a short stack. Ask the class to notice & wonder; land on: *“How many cups, stacked, to reach my height?”* Everyone records an estimate + a too-low and too-high.

“What do you need?” Students request the teacher’s height and measure a cup. The trap: stacking is NOT height × number — each added cup only contributes its *rim* (~1.5 cm), not its full ~12 cm. Students grapple toward a rule like `total = 1.5n + base`. Many paths: tables, a graph, repeated addition, an equation. Work at vertical whiteboards in random groups.

Actually stack cups to the teacher’s height and count — payoff against the estimates. Then **consolidate** with the 5 Practices: select a table, a graph, and an equation; sequence and connect them to surface the difference between a *proportional* (`y = mx`) and a *linear* (`y = mx + b`) relationship. Sequel: “How many to reach the ceiling? To reach the tallest student?”

blocks.text: Why it’s rich: a low floor (everyone can estimate and stack), a high ceiling (linear vs. proportional, slope as the rim height), genuinely multiple paths, and a satisfying reveal.
Finding & building tasks (so this isn’t extra invention every night)

items: **Use existing libraries:** Make Math Moments (the original reference for this toolbelt), Dan Meyer’s Three-Act catalog, Open Middle, Youcubed, Illustrative Mathematics — and the rich tasks already inside your adopted curriculum.
**“Three-act-ify” a textbook problem** you already have:

yes.title: …into a rich task
items: **Strip the information** — start with a picture or scenario, no numbers
**Withhold the question** — let students wonder it, and estimate first
**Let them request** what they need, and solve more than one way

no.title: From a typical word problem…
items: All numbers given up front
The question stated
One implied method

blocks.text: Setting it up to run well

items: **Name the math goal** the task serves (don’t pick a task just because it’s fun — pick it because it develops a specific understanding).
**Anticipate** strategies and misconceptions in your PLC beforehand.
**Use vertical non-permanent surfaces & visibly random groups** — more starts, more visible thinking, easier monitoring.
**Lean on Talk Moves and the “When to Tell” guide** — hold the tell during the struggle; the consolidation is the big, planned tell.
**Protect time for Act 3.** If you run out of time before consolidating, the task did not teach — budget for the reveal and the connect.
**Choose entry-friendly numbers and a visual hook** so a newcomer MLL can notice, wonder, and estimate alongside everyone.
**Random groups + vertical whiteboards** distribute status and make every group’s thinking visible — harder to hide, easier to value many approaches.
**Scaffold access, not demand:** add visuals, partners, and stems; do *not* hand struggling students a watered-down task.
**Sequence student work from accessible to sophisticated** in the consolidation so more students see their thinking honored on the way up.

blocks.text: Start with **one rich task per unit** once openers are established — not a daily practice and not before the discourse norms exist. Grow frequency as facilitation strengthens. See the rollout plan’s readiness trigger for the signal that your faculty is ready to begin.
Where this leads

This is the destination, not a way station. When rich tasks run regularly — students reasoning, teachers consolidating with the 5 Practices — you have arrived at the vision: every student developing all five strands through reasoning, struggle, and discourse around genuine mathematics. The openers were the rehearsal; this is the performance.
